newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bonn, Paris can both claim pact win - German media.
newsitem.headline: Bonn, Paris can both claim pact win - German media.

text.p: German newspapers on Tuesday said approval by European Union leaders of a controversial budget stability pact and a supplementary jobs accord could be claimed as a victory for both Bonn and Paris.

"The newly reached compromise can be presented by both Bonn and Paris as a success. The euro will stay stable, Finance Minister Theo Waigel will say, and his French counterpart will claim the stress on jobs as a victory in the fight against unemployment," wrote Die Welt daily.

But most commentators stressed the fact that Bonn's pet stability pact had been sealed on the first day of a two-day summit in Amsterdam without an addendum on job creation or the promise of new cash from Europe for jobs.
"The German gift to their French partners does not lock in new powers for the central EU organs or fresh money for job-creation programmes," wrote the conservative Frankfurter Allgemeine daily.

"But there is no reason for celebration. The solution is just like most Brussels compromises: it is too thin to have any durability. It helps the French to save face at home. But it will not be of much use either to them or their partners."
The Frankfurter Rundschau said the accord on coordinating job creation in Europe was -- like previous state attempts to boost employment -- "a paper tiger, regardless of what paper it is written on".

The mass circulation Bild daily said the accord showed that the political determination to introduce economic and monetary union (EMU) was unbroken and added that Chancellor Helmut Kohl had shown how much Bonn needed strong government.

"With a weaker Chancellor than Helmut Kohl the summit could have been very expensive for tax payers. A flash in the pan for the jobs market would have made the euro weak and above all cost our money," it wrote.
Bonn's General Anzeiger agreed with German politicians that the structural problems of inflexible labour markets could only be solved by national governments.

"Decisive is that the future single currency community decided on a stability pact that guarantees a strong euro. Otherwise employment problems would just have got worse -- despite any jobs pacts," it wrote.
But the Westdeutsche Allgemeine said the dispute between Paris and Bonn over the stability pact was just a foretaste of what would come after the launch of the single currency.

"The arguments about monetary policy, about the sense of a stable currency and the way of handling state debts will continue. They will even become more intense when the currency union actually starts," it predicted.
"This is all the result of the fundamental weakness of the currency union -- that it is lacking the necessary political basis," it added.
